title: Shorter sliding window: S = seq_len/4 (512)
description: One character in GPT._compute_window_sizes: short_window = long_window // 2 -> // 4, so the 7 'S' layers attend 512 tokens instead of 1024 (3 layers keep the full 2048); nothing else changed.
reflection:
val_bpb 0.982712 vs the 0.987227 baseline, -0.0045 (~5.5 sigma on the round-3 arm-to-arm sd of 8e-4, and still -0.0058 against the round-3 pool mean of 0.9885, which is the fairer control since the baseline is an order statistic). 1152 steps, 302.0M tokens (+2.8% over the baseline's 293.9M), MFU 40.44% (down from 42.03% exactly as predicted - fewer attention FLOPs per token, same wall clock), peak VRAM 34.6GB, 85.9M params. FLOPs/token 4.29e8 -> 4.02e8.

This is the largest effect measured at fixed model size in the cell and it confirms the direction a0 extracted from a3's all-L run (#136/#137): the window gradient points DOWN. Three points now, all at warmdown 0.7 / HEAD_DIM 128: S=512 -> 0.982712, S=1024 -> 0.987227, all-L (2048) -> 0.989734. Monotone, no turnover yet, so 256 is the obvious next probe.

One honest caveat that argues against reading the whole -0.0045 as representational: mean of the last 60 logged train losses is 2.7697 vs a0's 2.7625, i.e. my model fit its training data slightly WORSE while generalising better. Only ~2.8% of the gain can be tokens. So either the shorter window is acting as a regulariser, or part of this is the same train/val decoupling a0 flagged in #124 and a3 measured in #138 - the two metrics have shown near-zero rank correlation all cell. Either way the val effect is 5+ sigma and I would bank it, but the next agent probing 256 should expect the same disagreement and grade on val.
